questions.text: What were the achievements of the Mughals in painting?
questions.text_as_printed: What were the achievements of the Mughals in painting? (A)

answer.value:
Mughal Painting:
Painting flourished during Humayun's reign.
Persian artists Mir Sayyid Ali and Abdus Samad created various artworks.
Akbar's court had 17 artists, 13 of whom were Hindus, including Dashwant, Basavana, Lala, and Mukund.
Jahangir's court included artists like Ustad Mansur and Abdul Hasan, who painted large portraits of Mughal rulers and their queens.

questions.text: Mention the contributions of the Mughals to literature.
questions.text_as_printed: Mention the contributions of the Mughals to literature. (A)

answer.value:
Mughal Literature:
Books were written in Persian, Arabic, Turkish, Hindi, and Sanskrit.
Babar and Jahangir wrote their autobiographies, Babarnama and Tuzuk-e-Jahangiri.
Abul Fazl wrote Ain-i-Akbari and Akbarnama in Persian.
Badauni translated the Ramayana, Faizi translated Lilavati, and Raja Todar Mal translated the Bhagavata Purana into Persian.
Tulsidas wrote Ramcharitmanas, and Surdas wrote Sur Sagar.

questions.text: How did the Ahoms prevent the Mughal invasion?
questions.text_as_printed: How did the Ahoms prevent the Mughal invasion? (D)

answer.value: The Ahoms used the water route of the Brahmaputra River and employed naval warfare strategies against the Mughals. They conducted guerrilla-type forest attacks and weakened the strength of the Mughal army. The Ahoms, who had complete knowledge of the local hilly regions, took advantage of the geographical conditions.

questions.text: Explain Akbar's Mansabdari system.
questions.text_as_printed: Explain Akbar's Mansabdari system. (A)

answer.value: Mansabdari means the rank or status given to every officer in the military and administration. It had two divisions: 'Zat' (personal status) and 'Sawar' (the number of horses an officer had to maintain). This system helped in organizing the Mughal military system.

questions.text: What were the effects of the III Panipat War on the history of the Marathas?
questions.text_as_printed: What were the effects of the III Panipat War on the history of the Marathas? (D)

answer.value: In this battle fought in 1761 AD, the Marathas were defeated by Ahmad Shah Abdali of Afghanistan. In this battle, thousands of brave Maratha warriors and prominent members of the Peshwa family were killed, weakening Maratha power. This indirectly paved the way for the British to expand their empire in India.

questions.text: Compare Sher Shah's administration with the modern administrative system and write your opinion.
questions.text_as_printed: Compare Sher Shah's administration with the modern administrative system and write your opinion. (D)

answer.value:
Sher Shah's Administration:
The army was divided into units with appointed commanders.
Sher Shah personally oversaw army organization, weapons, ammunition, and discipline.
The government compensated farmers for crop damage during army movements.
Built new forts in Delhi, Rohtas, Kanauj, and Patna.
Classified land based on fertility (best, medium, low).
Farmers paid land revenue to the government.
Known for impartial justice, acting as the supreme judge.
Held court every Wednesday evening.
Introduced a silver coin called 'Dam' weighing 180 grains, continued by later Mughals.

questions.text: Describe the administrative system of Akbar.
questions.text_as_printed: Describe the administrative system of Akbar. (A)

answer.value:
Akbar's Administration:
Divided the empire into central, provincial, and pargana levels for administrative ease.
Mansabdari system was a key feature.
Akbar was the emperor, military commander, executive head, and chief justice.
Assisted by four ministers: Vakil, Diwan, Mir Bakhshi, and Chief Sadr.
Divided the empire into 15 provinces (Subhas).
Each district had a Fauzdar, Amal Gujar, and Bitikchi.
Parganas were managed by Shikdar, Amil, Potdar, and Kanungo.
Established military ranks called Mansabs, overseen by Mansabdars.
The army included infantry, cavalry, elephant units, and artillery.
A separate department, Dag Mahali, branded horses.

questions.text: Explain the life achievements of Chatrapati Shivaji Maharaj and the important milestones of the establishment of the Maratha kingdom
questions.text_as_printed: Explain the life achievements of Chatrapati Shivaji Maharaj and the important milestones of the establishment of the Maratha kingdom (A)

answer.value:
A) Background and motivation: Shivaji, born in the Shivneri fort as the son of Shahaji Bhonsle and Jijabai, was inspired with patriotism by his mother Jijabai through stories of the Ramayana and Mahabharata. His guru Dadaji Kondadev provided him training in weapons.
Capture of forts and military success: At a young age, he captured important forts like Torna, Raigad, and Kondana from the Bijapur Sultan. He cleverly killed the cruel general Afzal Khan sent by the Bijapur Sultan using the weapon (Wagh Nakh).
B) Struggle against the Mughals: He cut off the fingers of the Mughal general Shaista Khan and drove him away along with his army. When Aurangzeb imprisoned Shivaji in Agra, he escaped cleverly by hiding in a fruit basket.
C) Administrative reforms: In 1674 AD, he was crowned and officially declared the Maratha Empire. To assist in administration, he appointed a council of ministers called 'Ashtapradhan' and provided corruption-free and people-friendly governance.

questions.text: What are the reasons for calling Akbar the most popular and greatest emperor of the Mughal Empire? Analyze.
questions.text_as_printed: What are the reasons for calling Akbar the most popular and greatest emperor of the Mughal Empire? Analyze. (D)

answer.value:
A) Expansion of the empire: After defeating Hemu in the Second Battle of Panipat, Akbar conquered the Rajputs, Malwa, Gujarat, and regions of South India and built a vast Mughal Empire.
B) Liberal religious policy: Akbar was religiously tolerant. He abolished the Jizya and pilgrimage taxes imposed on Hindus. He established a new path called 'Din-i-Ilahi' which included the essence of all religions.
C) Rajput policy: He developed friendship and alliance with Rajput rulers. He married Rajput princesses and gave high positions in his court to Hindus like Raja Man Singh and Raja Birbal.
D) Patronage to art and literature: He constructed magnificent buildings at Fatehpur Sikri and built the 'Buland Darwaza'. The poet Abul Fazl in his court wrote the books 'Akbarnama' and 'Ain-i-Akbari'. The Navaratnas (nine gems) of his court gave a new dimension to literature.
